title: Protractor Axiom
summary: This Birkhoff-style degree-based supplement assigns each ray on a chosen side of a line a unique coordinate from 0° to 180°.
statements: Given a point O, a line through O, a chosen half-plane bounded by that line, and a choice of one boundary ray as 0°, the rays from O in that half-plane together with its two boundary rays match up one-to-one with the real numbers from 0° through 180°. The chosen boundary ray has coordinate 0° and its opposite ray has coordinate 180°.

The correspondence preserves order: if two rays form a nonstraight angle and a third ray lies in its interior, the third ray's coordinate lies strictly between the coordinates of the angle's two sides.

If two rays in this coordinate system have coordinates a° and b°, then the angle between them has size (b - a)° when a < b, and size (a - b)° when b < a. This angle size depends only on the two rays, not on the coordinate system used to calculate it.
Two angles are congruent exactly when they have the same angle size.

historicalContext.title: A degree-based supplement
paragraphs: Euclid and Hilbert compared angles through congruence rather than assigning every angle a real-number coordinate. In 1932, George David Birkhoff published a shorter metric foundation for plane geometry based on numerical scale and protractor readings.

This app retains a synthetic point-line and congruence foundation while borrowing a Birkhoff-style protractor axiom for numerical angle size. It is presented as a supplement because it adds degree coordinates rather than replacing the geometric core.

whatItEnables: A chosen initial ray, half-plane, and angle size determine exactly one ray. Angle addition follows from coordinate differences, and a straight angle has size 180°.
